messages.author: de80047cbc18c87e
messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Quality factor Q
parts:
library(tuneR)
library(seewave)
s <- readWave("S.wav")

. Solution 1: to focus around the dominant frequency by using the function cutspec()
fspec <- spec(s, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
fspec <- cutspec(fspec, flim=c(0,3))
Q(fspec)

. Solution 2: to compute the spectrum at a specific time position:
dfspec <- spec(s, at= 0.1, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
Q(dfspec)

. Solution 3: to compute the meanspectrum:
mfspec <- meanspec(s, dB="max0", plot=FALSE)
Q(mfspec)

Solution 1 returns very different results than solutions 2 and 3 dues to the frequency resolution of the spectrum.

I understand this is not an optimal solution but I cannot identify rightnow the bug probably linked to the length (number of frequency samples) of the spectrum.

HTH a bit

Jerome

parts:
Hello Jerome 
Firstly, many thanks for this r package - it will be extremely useful.

I'm working with Melanie and I have encountered more problems with the Q function.  I want to evaluate Q for a number of peaks within the signal so I cut the spectrum around each peak and then apply the Q function on the cut spectrum.  (I'm currently working with mathematically generated waves - modelling sound recordings from impact excitation method measurements - so I know exactly what peaks and Q values I should be getting)

I see in the help file that cutspec is supposed to be for a spectral analysis "not in dB" - but it does seem to work OK (I'm using  dB="max0") and I see you suggest the same in your answer to Melanie.  However, when I apply the Q function the frequency scale gets messed up - and the resulting values of dominant frequency and Q-factor are wrong.

Example:  Here I have cut the spectrum (in dB) around a peak at 8.05 kHz (the x-axis is in kHz and the y-axis is in dB).  The points are plotted from the cut spectrum and the lines are plotted from the original spectrum (this shows the cut worked correctly)


However, when I apply the Q function on this cut spectrum, the frequency range is changed.  This is what I get when I don't specify the sampling rate (which is 44100 Hz) in the Q command (the apparent frequency range runs from 0 to ~9kHz)



And this is what I get when I do specify the sampling rate in the Q command (the apparent frequency range runs from 0 to ~22kHz)
In both cases the Q-factor comes out the same (as the spectra are simply scaled) but the dominant frequency is reported differently.  This Q-factor is wrong of course because the spectrum does not really begin at zero.  The correct value of Q-factor is 200.  When I run the Q function on the whole spectrum of a wav containing only the frequency I am interested in, the Q-factor comes out to be very close to the true value. **As long as I analyse the whole wave and use a rectangular window** (the hanning window applied on all or part of the wave seems to run into problems...including the one Melanie reported at the top which seems to happen when the Q-factor is high)

Attached some example wav files.  The true frequency (Hz) and Q-factor values as as listed in the file name.  I'm trying to work with multiple frequencies (hence the wav with three components).  


I am guessing that the problem with the cut spectrum is related to this line in the function script (assumes the spectrum begins at zero I think)


range <- c(f/2000/length(spec), f/2000)

(sorry - I am not yet smart enough with R to suggest a solution to the script.  I've only been using it for one day. Perhaps it will be better to specify frequency range of interest within the Q function so you don't need to cut the spectrum and you don't get confusion across multiple peaks as below)




Many thanks 
Dan

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Quality factor Q
parts:
Further - I tried using the bandpass filter (ffilter) to reduce the wave to just the frequencies of interest, allowing then the Q function to be run on the whole spectrum. This does not always work because sometimes the Q-factor function returns a NA for $fmax or a numeric(0) for $fmin (or both).  This seems to happen when the peak is steep.

I wonder if it is related to the way that range is calculated. The line:

range <- c(f/2000/length(spec), f/2000)

give range slightly differently than in the spectrum - which seems to run from zero not f/2000/length(spec)

I am guessing that this results in a problem when you cut the interpolated spectrum either side of the maximum value.  If the cut is made one point (in the original spectrum) along from where it should be, then a very steep peak might not contain the point (in the cut interpolated spectrum) where it crosses the -3dB line.

(To check this theory, I tried changing the level to, say, -6bB ...and then the function works when previously it didn't)

Also, I am curious for the reason to round the maximum value of spec1 in this line
level2 <- round(max(spec1), 1) + level
Is it necessary to round it?

Thanks
Dan

PS, sorry: I made a typo in the file name above for the frequency combination wave.  It should be:
440 Hz with Q 80
8050 Hz with Q 200
9000 Hz with Q 2000

parts:
Sorry for yet another message - but now I have worked out how to write my own functions in R I was able to test.
The attached script works (changes from the function in the package are marked with #)

I have corrected the offset in the spectrum
And I have added more points to the interpolation

I think adding more points to the interpolation works here because the interpolated spectrum is also not quite correctly mapped to the frequency.  I haven't figured out how to properly fix it yet (other than by reducing the size of the error by adding more points)

The spectrum runs from 0 to F in n points of frequency.  Frequency for row i in the vector = (i-1)*F/(n-1)  

A cut spectrum runs from A to B in m points of frequency.  Frequency for row i in the vector = (i-1)*(B-A)/(m-1)+A  


Dan
